entries.note: Pokorny 746 has exactly 'mizdhó- ‚Lohn, Sold‘' with av. mīžda-, np. muzd, gr. misthós, Got. mizdō; Watkins/AHD prints the same root as 'mizdho-. Reward. [Pok. mizdho- 746]'. Modern Wiktionary writes it *misdʰós and analyses it as *mey-s- 'exchange' + *dʰeh₁- 'put' (i.e. 'what is put in exchange'), so the root, the language label 'Indo-European' and the gloss 'reward' are all right; only the notation differs (Nourai keeps Pokorny's -zdh-). The one weak point on the page is the Avestan node's second word mīžda-vare, which is not an attested Avestan compound (see node 1).

nodes.derivation: Av. mīžda- n. 'reward, wage' is the direct Iranian continuation of PIE *misdʰós: the PIE cluster *-zdʰ- gives Avestan -žd- and the vowel is lengthened before it (Y.44.18 tat mīždəm hanānī, Y.46.19, Y.55.3). Bartholomae, Altiran. Wb. col. 1187 s.v. mizda- glosses it 'Lohn als das verabredete oder zugesicherte oder gebührende Äquivalent einer Leistung', i.e. exactly 'reward, wage' — confirmed. The second word, mîžda-vare 'wage earner', is NOT an attested Avestan compound: the only Avestan derivative in -va(nt)- is mīžda-vant- 'provided with (the deserved) reward' (BRT col. 1188), and a grep of the whole of Bartholomae yields only mižda-, mižda-vant-/mizdavan̰t- and the case forms mizdahe/mizdavqn. Nourai's -vare is retro-projected from the well attested Middle Persian mizd-war 'hireling' (MacKenzie 1971:59 'mizd ... ~war [-wbl | N -ār] hireling'), whose second element does go back to *bara- 'bearing' (PIE *bʰer-), so his cross-reference ☞Bher 1 is right in substance but the form should be starred as Old Iranian *mīžda-bara-, not printed as Avestan.

nodes.derivation: All three are one family. NP مزد mozd < MP mizd [m(y)zd] 'reward, hire, pay' (MacKenzie 1971:59; Nyberg II s.v. mizd) < Old Iranian *miždam = Av. mīžda-; the Avestan/OIr. cluster -žd- was de-palatalised to -zd- in the SW (Persian) line. مزدور mozdur is inherited from MP mizd-war 'hireling' (MacKenzie 1971:59; Junker's muzdwar quoted in Mo'in's footnote to Borhan p. 2001) = mizd + -war < *bara- 'bearing' (PIE *bʰer-), with the regular MP -war > NP -ūr/-vār. مژده mužde 'good news' keeps the ž because it comes not from the SW form but from a NW/Parthian one: Parthian mwjdg /muždag/ '(good) news, message' > NP mužda, plus the Persian nominal -a; Horn (Grundriss no. 978, p. 219) already treated 'muzd, mužd ‘Lohn, Preis’, mužde (mizde) ‘frohe Botschaft’' as one entry and remarked 'Das u im Neupersischen ist auffällig' (i.e. *mizd would be expected; the u is by labialisation before the cluster). The semantic step is 'reward' > 'the reward paid to the bringer of good news' > 'good news' — still visible in مژدگانی moždegāni (mužde + -gān + -ī) 'the present given for good tidings' (Borhan p. 2005 n. 1, comparing Kurdish mizdgānī). Nourai's chart is right on every count.

nodes.derivation: Sogdian myzd /mizd/ 'wage, reward', written in the Sogdian (S) script, continues Old Iranian *miždam like MP mizd: Sogdian keeps the cluster as -zd- and shows the same i-vocalism, so it is a sister form of the Middle Persian word rather than a Persian loan. It is attested in the Ancient Letters (2.48-49, i.e. the early-4th-c. Sogdian merchant letters from Dunhuang) and discussed by Bailey, Prolexis 280. Gharib's Sogdian Dictionary no. 5675, p. 227, gives 'myzd S | mizd ? ©Av. mizda | salary, reward' — with the same comparison to Avestan mīžda- that Nourai draws.

nodes.derivation: The Germanic node is right in substance but the form is a conflation. Proto-Germanic had *mizdō (f.) 'reward', preserved unchanged in Gothic mizdō (Klein p. 957; Pokorny 746). In West Germanic the *z was rhotacised and then lost before *d with compensatory lengthening (*mizdō > Proto-West-Germanic *miʀdu > *mēdu), giving Old English mēd beside the archaic non-syncopated meord/meard, Old Saxon mēda, Old High German mēta/miata, German Miete 'rent'. Watkins/AHD accordingly writes 'West Germanic *mēdē-'. Nourai's 'medo' is that West Germanic *mēdō/*mēdē- spelled without the length mark, and so skips the Gothic-type *mizdō stage; as a label for the branch immediately above English meed it is acceptable, but 'Germanic *mizdō' would be the correct reconstruction at this level.
nodes.derivation_fa: این گره در اصل درست است ولی صورت آن آمیزه‌ای است. ژرمنی آغازین *mizdō «پاداش» داشته که در گوتی بی‌دگرگونی mizdō مانده است (کلاین ص ۹۵۷؛ پوکورنی ص ۷۴۶). در ژرمنی غربی z به r بدل و سپس پیش از d افتاده و واکه در جبران آن کشیده شده است (*mizdō > *miʀdu > *mēdu)؛ از این‌رو انگلیسی کهن mēd (و صورت کهن‌تر meord)، ساکسون کهن mēda، آلمانی علیای کهن mēta/miata و آلمانی Miete پدید آمده‌اند. واتکینز در ضمیمهٔ AHD همین را «ژرمنی غربی *mēdē-» می‌نویسد. صورت «medo» نورایی همان *mēdō ژرمنی غربی بدون نشانهٔ کشش است و مرحلهٔ *mizdō را نادیده می‌گیرد؛ با احتیاط پذیرفتنی است.

nodes.derivation: English meed 'reward, recompense' (now only poetic/archaic) is inherited, not borrowed: Old English mēd (West Saxon; beside meord, meard, meorþ) > Middle English mede, meede > meed, with the regular ME ē > ModE /iː/ and the <ee> spelling. It is the direct English reflex of West Germanic *mēdu < Proto-Germanic *mizdō < PIE *misdʰós, hence a cognate of German Miete 'rent' and of Persian mozd. Klein and Skeat both give the chain, and Watkins's index lists 'MEED mizdho-'.

entries.note: The Semitic root and its gloss are right: Arabic مِلْح milḥ, Hebrew מֶלַח melaḥ, Aramaic מִלְחָא milḥā, Syriac melḥā and Maltese melħ all go back to Proto-West-Semitic *milḥ- 'salt' (Klein p. 928 s.v. mallow gives the same set, adding 'Akkad. milu' — the Akkadian everyday word is in fact ṭābtu, milʾu being 'saltpetre'). What is NOT right on this chart is the Indo-European half of it: Nourai (following Klein, who follows H. Lewy 1895) makes Latin malva and Greek malachē direct borrowings from Hebrew mallūaḥ. Modern scholarship rejects this: Watkins/AHD — Nourai's own reference for the malachite node — says 'Greek malakhḗ ... akin to Latin malva, both probably borrowed from a pre-Indo-European Mediterranean language', and Etymonline and Wiktionary say the same, noting in addition that the Semitic mallūaḥ plants are Amaranthaceae (saltbush) and not Malvaceae. Nodes 4 and 6 are therefore marked disputed. The Málaga branch (nodes 8-12) is an independent and older hypothesis that remains possible but is not proven (see node 8).
entries.note_fa: ریشهٔ سه‌حرفی سامی م‌ل‌ح و معنای «نمک» درست است: عربی مِلْح، عبری melaḥ، آرامی milḥā، سریانی melḥā و مالتی melħ همه از *milḥ- سامیِ غربی آغازین‌اند (کلاین ص ۹۲۸ همین‌ها را آورده است). آنچه درست نیست نیمهٔ هندواروپایی نمودار است: نورایی به پیروی از کلاین (و او به پیروی از ه. لِوی ۱۸۹۵) malva لاتین و malachē یونانی را وام‌واژهٔ بی‌واسطهٔ عبری mallūaḥ می‌داند. پژوهش امروزی این را رد می‌کند؛ واتکینز در ضمیمهٔ AHD — همان مرجعی که خودِ نورایی برای «malachite» به آن ارجاع داده — می‌گوید یونانی malakhḗ و لاتین malva «هر دو احتمالاً از زبانی مدیترانه‌ای پیش‌هندواروپایی وام گرفته شده‌اند»؛ اتیمونلاین و ویکی‌واژه نیز همین را می‌گویند و می‌افزایند که گیاهانِ سامیِ mallūaḥ از تیرهٔ اسفناجیان‌اند نه پنیرکیان. پس گره‌های ۴ و ۶ «رد‌شده» نشان زده‌اند. شاخهٔ مالاگا (گره‌های ۸ تا ۱۲) فرضیه‌ای کهن و ممکن ولی اثبات‌ناشده است.

nodes.derivation: Arabic مِلْح milḥ (m., pl. أَمْلَاح ʔamlāḥ / مِلَاح milāḥ) 'salt' belongs to the root م ل ح (m-l-ḥ) and is inherited from Proto-West-Semitic *milḥ- — not derived from any other Semitic language, i.e. the arrow 'Semitic root → Arabic' is simply the normal relation of a root to its qatl-pattern noun (*miCC- > milḥ). It is Qurʾānic (25:53 hāḏā ʿaḏbun furātun wa-hāḏā milḥun ʔujāj 'this one sweet and fresh, that one salty and bitter'). The same root gives مَلَحَ malaḥa 'to salt', مَالِح/مَلِيح 'salty', and the transferred senses 'wit, grace, beauty' that Persian later borrowed (see node 2).

nodes.derivation: Persian مِلح melh 'salt' is a straightforward Arabic loan (an Arabism of the learned, medical and alchemical registers); the inherited Persian word is نمک namak < MP namak, and melh never displaced it in ordinary speech. Moʿin's Farhang marks it '[ع.] (اِ.) نمک. ج. املاح و ملاح' — Arabic, noun, 'salt', plural amlāḥ/milāḥ — and Dehkhoda quotes Muntahā al-arab and the medical literature (ملح اندرانی, ملح طبرزد, ملح بول …). The forms Nourai adds in the margin are the same Arabic stem borrowed with its own morphology: أملاح amlāḥ (broken plural, in Persian 'salts' as a chemical term), مَلاحت malāḥat (maṣdar of the ii-form, 'saltiness' > 'gracefulness, comeliness'), ملیح/ملیحه malīḥ/malīḥa (faʿīl adjective, 'salty' > 'comely, pretty') — the same 'salt → wit/beauty' shift that Arabic itself made.
nodes.derivation_fa: «مِلح» در فارسی وام‌واژهٔ عربی است و در لایهٔ ادبی، طبی و کیمیایی به کار می‌رفته؛ واژهٔ میراثی فارسی «نمک» (از namak پهلوی) است و «ملح» هرگز جای آن را در زبان روزمره نگرفت. فرهنگ معین آن را «(مِ) [ع.] (اِ.) نمک. ج. املاح و ملاح» ثبت کرده و دهخدا از منتهی‌الارب و متون طبی شاهد آورده است (ملح اندرانی، ملح طبرزد، ملح بول…). صورت‌های حاشیه‌ای نمودار همه از همان ستاک عربی‌اند: «املاح» جمع مکسر (در فارسی اصطلاح شیمی)، «ملاحت» مصدرِ بابِ دوم به معنی «شوری» و سپس «نمکینی و زیبایی»، «ملیح/ملیحه» صفت بر وزن فعیل به معنی «شور» و سپس «نمکین، زیبا» — همان تحول معناییِ «نمک ← نمکینی/زیبایی» که در خودِ عربی رخ داده است. ادعای نورایی درست است.

nodes.derivation: Hebrew מֶלַח melaḥ 'salt' (absolute state; construct מְלַח) is inherited from Proto-West-Semitic *milḥ-, exactly parallel to Arabic milḥ — confirmed. מַלּוּחַ mallūaḥ, a maqqūl-type derivative of the same root ('the salty one'), occurs once in the Hebrew Bible, Job 30:4, and its formation from melaḥ is not in doubt. The gloss is what is loose: mallūaḥ is the saltbush / orach Atriplex halimus, a halophyte of the Amaranthaceae (Aramaic mallūḥā, Arabic مُلَّاح mullāḥ 'seepweed' are the same plant); 'mallows' is the King James rendering of Job 30:4 which Klein, and after him Nourai, carried over. The true mallow (Malva) is a Malvaceae and a different plant, which is one of the reasons the borrowing claimed in nodes 4 and 6 is now rejected.
nodes.derivation_fa: عبری מֶלַח melaḥ «نمک» میراثِ *milḥ- سامیِ غربی آغازین است و درست با مِلْح عربی برابر می‌ایستد؛ این بخش پذیرفتنی است. מַלּוּחַ mallūaḥ نیز مشتقی از همین ریشه («شوره‌ای») است و یک بار در کتاب ایوب (۳۰:۴) آمده؛ ساخته شدنش از melaḥ تردیدی ندارد. آنچه دقیق نیست معنای آن است: mallūaḥ همان «سلمهٔ شوره‌زار» (Atriplex halimus) از تیرهٔ اسفناجیان است (آرامی mallūḥā و عربی مُلّاح همان گیاه)، و برگردانِ «پنیرک» از ترجمهٔ انگلیسی شاه جیمز به کلاین و از او به نورایی رسیده است. پنیرکِ راستین (Malva) از تیرهٔ پنیرکیان و گیاهی دیگر است؛ همین ناهمخوانی گیاه‌شناختی یکی از دلیل‌های ردِ وام‌گیریِ ادعاشده در گره‌های ۴ و ۶ است.

nodes.derivation: Latin malva 'mallow' is real and is the ancestor of the Romance and English words, but the arrow drawn here — straight from Hebrew mallūaḥ — is not the modern view, on two counts. (i) Source: Watkins/AHD (p. 39 of the 1985 edition, the same appendix Nourai cites as AHD:1527 for malachite) brackets malakhḗ as non-Indo-European and says Greek malakhḗ and Latin malva are 'both probably borrowed from a pre-Indo-European Mediterranean language'; Etymonline says of malva 'a word from a Mediterranean substrate language. The same lost word apparently yielded Greek malakhe'; Beekes and Chantraine treat μαλάχη as Pre-Greek (the α/ο and χ/κ alternations malákhē / molókhē are a Pre-Greek signature). The Semitic explanation goes back to H. Lewy, Die semitischen Fremdwörter im Griechischen (1895), 31 f., which is precisely what Klein p. 928 is quoting, and Wiktionary adds that the Semitic plants are Amaranthaceae, not Malvaceae. (ii) Route: even on the Semitic hypothesis Latin would have taken the word through Greek, as with most Mediterranean plant names, not directly from Hebrew. Verdict: disputed — the modern account is 'Mediterranean substrate word, shared by Greek and Latin'.
nodes.derivation_fa: لاتین malva «پنیرک» واژه‌ای واقعی و نیای واژه‌های رومانس و انگلیسی است، اما پیکانی که اینجا کشیده شده — یک‌راست از عبری mallūaḥ — دیدگاه امروزی نیست، از دو جهت: یک) سرچشمه: واتکینز در ضمیمهٔ AHD (چاپ ۱۹۸۵، ص ۳۹؛ همان ضمیمه‌ای که نورایی برای malachite به آن ارجاع می‌دهد) malakhḗ را با قلاب به نشانِ غیرهندواروپایی بودن آورده و می‌گوید یونانی malakhḗ و لاتین malva «هر دو احتمالاً از زبانی مدیترانه‌ای پیش‌هندواروپایی وام گرفته شده‌اند»؛ اتیمونلاین نیز malva را «واژه‌ای از زبانِ زیرلایهٔ مدیترانه‌ای» می‌داند و بیکس و شانترن μαλάχη را پیش‌یونانی می‌شمارند (جابه‌جایی α/ο و χ/κ در malákhē/molókhē نشانهٔ پیش‌یونانی است). فرضیهٔ سامی از ه. لِوی (۱۸۹۵، ص ۳۱ به بعد) است و کلاین (ص ۹۲۸) همان را نقل می‌کند. دو) مسیر: حتی با پذیرشِ فرضیهٔ سامی، لاتین این واژه را — مانند بیشترِ نام‌های گیاهیِ مدیترانه‌ای — از راه یونانی می‌گرفت نه بی‌واسطه از عبری. داوری: پژوهش امروزی این پیکان را رد می‌کند و به جای آن «واژهٔ زیرلایهٔ مدیترانه‌ای، مشترک میان یونانی و لاتین» می‌گوید.

nodes.derivation: Both English words come from Latin malva, but by two different routes and 800 years apart. mallow: Latin malva was borrowed into Old English as mealwe/malwe (it is in the OE herbals), giving Middle English malwe and, by a late-14th-century respelling of final -we as -ow, mallow. mauve: a modern loan from French mauve 'mallow' (< Latin malva), taken into English in 1856-59 as the name of the first aniline dye, W. H. Perkin's 'mauveine', so called from the mallow-flower colour; hence the colour term. Klein treats them in one family ('Cp. malachite, malvacious, mauve'), and Skeat's entry is simply 'Mauve, the name of a colour; see Mallow'. The Latin→English edge is not in doubt; only the Semitic origin further up (node 4) is.

nodes.derivation: The word is real: Ancient Greek μαλάχη malákhē (Attic/Ionic also μολόχη molókhē) 'mallow', attested from Hesiod and the Hippocratic corpus; Nourai's 'malaxe' is his transliteration with x for χ. What is disputed is the parentage. The α/ο alternation malákhē ~ molókhē together with the χ/κ variation (cf. μάλβακα in Hesychius) is a classic Pre-Greek signature, and that is how Beekes's Etymological Dictionary of Greek and Chantraine class the word; Watkins/AHD calls it 'probably borrowed from a pre-Indo-European Mediterranean language'; Wiktionary calls the etymology 'Uncertain', mentions the Semitic proposal (Hebrew mallūaḥ) and objects both that the Semitic plants are Amaranthaceae rather than Malvaceae and that the proposal ignores Middle Armenian բաղբակ and Georgian ბალბა, which point to a non-Semitic Mediterranean/Caucasian source. So the Hebrew → Greek arrow reflects H. Lewy 1895 via Klein and is not today's view.
nodes.derivation_fa: خودِ واژه واقعی است: یونانی باستان μαλάχη malákhē (در آتیک و ایونی نیز μολόχη molókhē) «پنیرک»، از هزیود و مجموعهٔ بقراطی به بعد گواهی شده؛ «malaxe» آوانگاریِ نورایی با x در برابر χ است. آنچه محل اختلاف است تبارِ آن است. جابه‌جاییِ α/ο در malákhē ~ molókhē همراه با تناوبِ χ/κ (سنجیده شود با μάλβακα در هزوخیوس) نشانهٔ کلاسیکِ واژه‌های پیش‌یونانی است و بیکس و شانترن آن را همین‌گونه دسته‌بندی می‌کنند؛ واتکینز آن را «احتمالاً وام از زبانی مدیترانه‌ای پیش‌هندواروپایی» می‌داند؛ ویکی‌واژه ریشه را «نامعلوم» می‌خواند، پیشنهادِ سامی (عبری mallūaḥ) را می‌آورد و دو ایراد می‌گیرد: ناهمخوانیِ تیرهٔ گیاهی، و نادیده گرفتنِ բաղբակ ارمنیِ میانه و ბალბა گرجی که به سرچشمه‌ای مدیترانه‌ای/قفقازی و نه سامی اشاره دارند. پس پیکانِ عبری ← یونانی بازتابِ نظر لِوی (۱۸۹۵) از راه کلاین است و پژوهش امروزی آن را نمی‌پذیرد.

nodes.derivation: The edge Greek → English is right, with the usual Romance staging. Greek μαλαχῖτις (λίθος) malakhîtis (líthos) 'mallow(-green) stone', a -ῖτις adjective from μαλάχη 'mallow', named for the resemblance of the mineral's green to mallow leaves, gave Latin molochitis (Pliny, NH 37.114) and then French malachite, whence English malachite in the late 14th century. Nourai's gloss is chemically right in substance: malachite is a basic copper carbonate, Cu2CO3(OH)2. Note that his own reference here — the AHD Indo-European appendix — makes the Greek word a pre-Indo-European Mediterranean loan, so the appendix supports this node while contradicting the Hebrew origin drawn at node 6.

nodes.derivation: The historical facts are solid: a Phoenician colony was founded on the site of modern Málaga by Tyrians about 770 BC, appears on its own coinage as Punic 𐤌𐤋𐤊𐤀 mlkʾ, and is Malaka/Malaca in Greek and Latin authors; Roman Malaca lived on fish-salting and garum. The etymology from the Semitic word for 'salt' — Klein p. 926: 'The name of Malaga, orig. a Phoenician colony, comes fr. Phoen. malha, ‘salt’, which is rel. to Heb. melah' — fits that industry and is the most frequently repeated explanation, but it is not proven: the Punic legend is written with kaph (mlkʾ), not with ḥeth, which is why other scholars connect the name instead with Semitic m-l-k 'king, royal' or take it as pre-Phoenician. Also 'malha' is Klein's citation form of the common noun, not an attested spelling of the toponym. Hence plausible, not confirmed; the node's language label 'Semitic' would be better as 'Phoenician/Punic'.

nodes.derivation: Spanish Málaga is the unbroken continuation of the Phoenician name of the same place: Punic mlkʾ / Greek Malaka > Latin Malaca (a confederated city under the Lex Flavia Malacitana, hence the adjective malacitano still used today) > Andalusi Arabic مالقة Mālaqa after the conquest of 711 > Castilian Málaga after the Castilian capture of the city in 1487. The stress on the first syllable and the -g- for Latin -c- are the normal Ibero-Romance treatment of the intervocalic voiceless stop in a name transmitted through Arabic. So the edge 'Phoenician toponym → Spanish' is right; only the further derivation of that toponym from 'salt' (node 8) is uncertain.

nodes.derivation: Persian مالاگا mālāgā for the Spanish port is a modern European loan, and the spelling itself shows which door it came through: the گ (g) can only render a European g, whereas the older Islamic-period Persian and Arabic form of the same city is مالقة Mālaqa with qāf (as in the Arabic geographers and in Persian works depending on them). A g-form therefore entered Persian in the 19th-20th century from French or English, which makes Nourai's route French → Persian plausible; but nothing in the form distinguishes French from English mediation, and Moʿin's Farhang vol. 6 (the aʿlām volumes), where he cites the entry, is not digitised, so the specific claim could not be checked against its own source.

nodes.derivation: English Malaga is the Spanish place name taken over unchanged except for the loss of the accent and the anglicised stress (/ˈmæləɡə/). Klein's headword is framed exactly this way — he defines Malaga as the wine and then explains the town's name — which is precisely Nourai's gloss 'a Spanish port and its famous wine'.

entries.note: Pokorny 747 has the root as 'moiso-s oder maiso-s ‚Schaf; Fließ, Fell, daraus gefertigte Schläuche, Säcke‘' — so the root name, the label 'Indo-European' and the gloss 'sheep' are all right; Nourai merely drops the second half of the meaning. That half matters, because it is what ties Sanskrit meṣá- 'ram, fleece' and Avestan maēša- to Old Church Slavonic měxŭ 'skin bag, bellows', Russian mekh 'fur', Lithuanian maĩšas 'net, sack' and Old Prussian moasis 'bellows' — the semantic bridge being the sheepskin. Wiktionary reconstructs it as *moysós and glosses it 'ram, sheep' and 'sheepskin, fleece, wool'.

nodes.derivation: The forms are right and so is the descent, but the two glosses are swapped in emphasis. Avestan maēša- is a masculine noun 'sheep, ram' and maēšī- its feminine 'ewe' — Bartholomae, Altiran. Wb. col. 1109: 'j. maēša- m.; maēšī- f. ‘Schaf; Schafmutter‘', with Yt. 14.33 maēšahe kəhrpa aurunahe 'in the shape of a wild ram' and A. 3.7 maēšīnąm ... paiti.puθranąm 'ewes with young'; Buck p. 158 likewise 'Av. maēša- ‘ram’ ..., Av. maēšī- ‘ewe’'. Nourai's 'mâěšî : sheep' should therefore be 'ewe'. Phonologically maēša- is the regular Iranian outcome of PIE *moysós: *oy > Avestan aē, *s after the diphthong becomes š (ruki), Sanskrit meṣá- shows the same. The transliteration mâěša/mâěšî is Nourai's own convention (â for a, ě for e) and is printed that way in the book, so it is not a scanning error.

nodes.derivation: NP میش mīš continues Middle Persian mēš (Book Pahlavi myš, e.g. in the compound mēš-sār 'of sheep-leather', MacKenzie 1971 and Nyberg II s.v.), from Old Iranian *maiša- = Avestan maēša-; the MP majhūl ē regularly becomes ī in New Persian spelling and in the modern standard pronunciation, which is exactly what Moʿin notes in his footnote on میش in Borhan: 'بکسر اول (تلفظ کنونی) و در تلفظ قدیم mēš، اوستایی maēša-' followed by the Baluchi, Wakhi and Sarikoli cognates. In current Persian میش is specifically the ewe (the ram being قوچ), so Nourai's 'ram' is a shade off; Horn's no. 1008 gives both senses ('Schaaf, Widder'). گاومیش gāvmīš 'water buffalo' is inherited as a whole from the Middle Persian compound gāw-mēš (PHD p. 38 'gāw-mēš [TWR Amyš | N gā(w)mēš] buffalo'), literally 'cow-sheep', a descriptive name for the animal introduced from India; the compound was borrowed out of Middle Iranian into Old Armenian գոմէշ gomēš, Syriac ܓܡܘܫܐ gāmōšā, Old Georgian ḳambeči and Arabic جاموس jāmūs. Ferdowsi's line quoted in the book (همه پایه‌ها چون سر گاومیش) shows the word in place by the 10th century.
